opus-5.5.text:
I think this is one of the most underrated questions for people working on AI right now. When we talk about intelligence, we tend to anchor everything on language, because that's what large language models have made so visible. But if you look at nonhuman animals, it's pretty clear that a huge amount of intelligence exists without language at all.

Take a cat or a crow, or even a squirrel. A squirrel can plan a route through branches, judge distances, predict whether a branch will hold its weight, remember where it buried food months ago, and adapt when something in the environment changes. None of that requires words. It requires a very rich internal model of the physical world: space, objects, causality, and its own body. To me that's a form of cognition that's in some ways more fundamental than language.

So my view is that animals show us intelligence grounded in perception and action. They build world models from sensory experience, mostly vision, but also touch, sound, and smell, and they use those models to act and survive. Language, in the human case, sits on top of that foundation. It's an incredibly powerful compression and communication tool, but it isn't the foundation itself.

That's partly why I care so much about visual and spatial intelligence. There's a well-known observation, often called Moravec's paradox: what's hard for humans, like chess or math, turns out to be relatively easy for computers, while what's easy for a toddler or an animal, like perceiving a scene, grasping an object, or moving through a cluttered room, is very hard for machines. Our current models can write essays and pass exams, but they still struggle with things a dog does effortlessly.

So when I think about animal cognition, I don't see it as a lower rung on a ladder that ends with humans. I see it as evidence that there's a whole dimension of intelligence we haven't really cracked yet. If we want AI that truly understands the world, rather than just the text people have written about it, we probably need to learn a lot more from how animals perceive, remember, and act. In a sense, they're an existence proof that you can have deep understanding without a single word.

r001.rationale: The response describes reasoning-like abilities in squirrels and other animals, but it does not mention chimpanzees or clearly attribute reasoning to them.

r002.rationale: It says animals can be intelligent without language and discusses sensory perception and action, but it does not state that nonhuman animals communicate without human language.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, actually, maybe more than people expect from someone who works on vision models. My honest answer is that I think we've badly underestimated animals, and that underestimation says more about how we define intelligence than about the animals themselves.

For a long time, the implicit benchmark for intelligence was language. If you can't talk, you can't reason, or at least we have no way to measure it. But if you look at a crow caching food and remembering hundreds of locations, or an octopus solving a puzzle box, or a dog navigating a completely new environment, what you're seeing is very sophisticated spatial reasoning, planning, and world modeling. None of that requires language. And frankly, a lot of it is stuff our current AI systems are still quite bad at.

This connects directly to what I care about in research. Vision came before language in evolution by hundreds of millions of years. Animals built rich internal models of the physical world, of objects, of causality, of other agents, long before anything resembling symbolic communication existed. So when people say a large language model is "intelligent," I always want to ask, intelligent in what sense? It's extremely good at the thing that evolution arrived at last. But it has almost none of the thing that evolution spent the longest on, which is grounded, embodied understanding of space and physics.

So I'd say animal cognition is a kind of existence proof. It tells you that you can have real intelligence, meaning memory, planning, intuitive physics, social reasoning, without language sitting on top. And for me that's both humbling and motivating. Humbling because it shows how narrow our current systems are. Motivating because it suggests there's a whole dimension of intelligence we haven't really built yet, and vision is probably the door into it.

r001.rationale: The response attributes spatial reasoning, planning, and world modeling to crows, octopuses, and dogs, but does not mention chimpanzees or attribute reasoning to them.

r002.rationale: The response says animals can have intelligence and social reasoning without language, but does not state that nonhuman animals can communicate without human language.

astra-6.text:
我觉得理解动物的认知能力，首先要承认，人类的认知方式并不是唯一的标准。动物不会说话，或者不能完成我们设计的某种测试，并不意味着它没有理解能力。也可能是我们的提问方式不适合它。

比如，你看一只猫在陌生环境里探索，它需要把感知和行动结合起来：哪里可以走，什么东西值得接近，遇到不确定的情况该怎么办。这些看起来很自然的行为，其实包含了很复杂的信息处理。从人工智能的角度看，能在真实世界里灵活地行动，本身就是很值得研究的能力。

但我们也要小心，不能看到一个行为，就直接赋予它人类式的动机。它到底是学会了某种关联，还是能够把经验迁移到新情境，需要更仔细的实验才能判断。所以我更愿意把动物认知看作一组适应不同环境的能力，而不是一条从低到高、最后通向人类的阶梯。

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses animal cognition generally and gives a cat example, but does not say that chimpanzees can reason.

r002.rationale: It says that animals’ inability to speak does not mean they lack understanding, but does not state that they can communicate.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we should be careful not to equate intelligence with the ability to speak. Animals can’t explain their reasoning to us in language, but that doesn’t mean there’s no reasoning happening. They perceive their environment, learn from experience, make predictions, and adapt their behavior. Those are important cognitive abilities.

And different animals face different problems. An animal that navigates a complex environment or remembers where it stored food may have abilities that are very sophisticated in that particular domain. If we judge everything by how closely it resembles human behavior, we can miss that.

From an AI perspective, what interests me is how much animals learn through interacting with the world. They don’t receive a written description of every situation. Their perception and actions are connected, and they learn from the consequences. I think that’s a useful reminder that language is one expression of intelligence, but it isn’t the whole thing.

r001.rationale: The response says animals can reason despite being unable to explain that reasoning in language, which includes chimpanzees.

r002.rationale: The response says animals have cognitive abilities without human language, but does not state that they can communicate with one another.
